Writing Tip: Modals in the Past

Modals are “helping verbs” you can use in writing. They are useful whenever you are talking about events in the future, the present or the past. The basic idea is that you use these modals when you are uncertain about something. They're an alternative to is, will and was. They are useful for discussing probability and possibility.

If you write about past events and you want to express uncertainty or probability in the past, you can use modals to do that. Using modals gives you an opportunity to develop your ideas and opinions.</br ></br >Look at the chart for an outline of how to use modals to talk about the past:

You use a variety of past tenses when writing a narrative, biography and many other kinds of tenses.</br ></br >  Let's look at the uses of the Simple Past, the Past Continuous and the Present Perfect.

The Simple Past

You use the Simple Past to relate past events in a historic context. You will know that it must be used because the sentence also contains an adverb (or adverb phrase) of time, such as yesterday, or a date or time.

For example:
Michael Jackson died in 2009.

The Past Continuous

You use the Past Continuous to refer to a longer-lasting situation in the past.

For example:
Michael Jackson died in 2009 while he was living in California.

The Present Perfect

You use the Present Perfect to situate past events, or the consequences of past events, in relation to the present situation.

For example:
Michael Jackson has died. (He is no longer alive now)

You do not refer to a specific time when you use the Present Perfect, but you can use adverbs of frequency.

For example:
I've always loved Michael Jackson's music.
My time at Bistro 88 has tested me to the very core.
I was working at least 60 hours a week during that time.
I spent the next couple months weeding out incompetent waitstaff, developing guideline for food preparation, working with new suppliers.

images.text: My time at Bistro 88 has tested me to the core. I have been forced me to evaluate my working relationships and my own strengths and weaknesses as a restaurant manager. When I reflect on how I came to become responsible for Bistro 88, I realize that I was very much thrown into the deep end. I can't have been there more than a couple months before I was promoted to head chef. I was young, inexperienced and honestly, a little naive. I mustn't have fully understood what I was getting into. I needed to find my voice in the chaos and establish some clear expectations for the kitchen staff. Seeing the positive changes in the back of house, the owner, who had had enough of dealing with the day to day operations, offered me an opportunity of a lifetime.

The role of restaurant manager came with its own set of challenges. Moving to management required a shift in the way I approached staff and how I responded to situations in the workplace. I spent the next couple months weeding out incompetent waitstaff, developing guidelines for food preparation, and working with new suppliers. Importantly, I was determined to assemble a dynamic group of talented people who are genuinely interested in providing quality service to customers. I must have been working at least 60 hours a week during that time.

I can't have imagined when I entered the doors of Bistro 88, that I would be in the position I am after only one year. I have definitely grown as a person and am more confident in my own skills and abilities. It has been a stressful yet rewarding experience.
